study.title: 2 Samuel 11 David, adultery, and the attempt to cover up sin
study.overview: The chapter narrates David's moral fall amid a successful military campaign. As Joab and the army surround Rabbah, David remains in Jerusalem, see Bathsheba, and sends her to seek her and commit adultery. When she becomes pregnant, David tries to hide guilt through maneuvers with Uriah, but the plan fails because Uriah shows himself loyal to the people, the ark and the companions at war. David then becomes even more guilty: he writes a letter determining the death of Uriah, and the plan is executed. After the mourning, David takes Bathsheba as a woman, but the chapter closes with the spiritual verdict: what David made displeased the LORD.

outline.title: David sees, desires and takes Bathsheba
outline.explanation: The chapter begins with David off the battlefield and in Jerusalem. From the terrace of the palace, he sees Bathsheba, sends to investigate who she is and takes her for herself. The text makes it clear that David's action was active and blameworthy, culminating in pregnancy and the need to hide sin.

outline.title: The attempt to cover up the guilt through Uriah
outline.explanation: David calls Uriah back from the war and tries to make him sleep with his wife, so that the pregnancy seems to be his. Uriah, however, refuses to enjoy domestic comfort while the ark, Israel, Judah, and the soldiers are campaigning. Even the drunkenness planned by David does not break Urias' allegiance.

outline.title: The Murder of Uriah and the Closure of Sin
outline.explanation: Failed the cover-up, David sends the commandment of his death by the hand of Uriah. Joab fulfills the plan, Uriah dies, and David responds with apparent coldness. After the mourning of Bathsheba, he takes her as a woman, but the chapter concludes with the divine assessment that all this displeased the LORD.

study.context: The text itself informs that this happened at the time the kings leave the war, that is, in a station appropriate for military campaigning. He also shows the siege to Rabbah and the presence of Joab in command. The notes note that David remained in Jerusalem while the others were in campaign, and that the environment of the terrace houses allowed to see what happened nearby.
study.theology: The chapter teaches, with great force, that spiritual privileges and previous deeds do not immunize anyone against serious fall. Sin here begins with omission and covetousness, then advances to adultery, lies, manipulation and murder. There is also an important moral contrast: Uriah, a Hittite, appears as a model of loyalty and integrity, while David, the king of Israel, acts with infidelity. The narrative shows that sin rarely becomes isolated; when guilt is welcomed and defended, it usually generates new evils. In the end, the phrase about the pleasure of the LORD indicates that God's assessment is decisive, even when the public appearance seems controlled. Evangelical reading tends to see here a serious warning about the need for true repentance, not just managing the consequences.

scholarViews.insight: David's failures occurred amidst great military success against the Ammonites, and the chapter darkens his career by showing that he remained in Jerusalem while he should be with the army.

The closing of the chapter points out that, although David had committed great sins, the Scriptures do not hide its flaws; this serves to warn readers and show that God does not treat such crimes with indulgence.
David wrote to Joab a letter that Uriah took with him, making this man the bearer of his own command that determined his death.

questions: What spiritual dangers do they appear when a person with a position and responsibilities moves away from the place where he should be?
How does Uriah's behavior further expose the contrast between human fidelity and David's sin?
Why is it so important to remember that the text ends with God's assessment, and not with the version that David tried to build?
study.practice: This chapter invites you to watch the first steps of sin: the look you want, the question concerned, the attempt to hide, rationalization and lies. In practice, this means quickly abandoning any path of cover-up and seeking sincere confession before God and affected people. It also calls us to value the integrity of Uriah: loyalty to the people of God, a sense of responsibility and refusal of selfish benefits in times of conflict. For leaders, the alert is even more serious: authority does not replace obedience.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text does not explicitly clarify whether Bathsheba acted voluntarily at each stage; the notes present cautious reading and even alternative on this, but the chapter concentrates its condemnation on David. There is also not enough basis here for detailing exact chronology, precise duration of grief or inferences beyond what the chapter and notes claim.
